title: Synthetic air handlers: a supply-air sensor reading 3 F high (generated by CAMBER)
summary: SYNTHETIC, generated locally by CAMBER (no download, no real building): two identical variable-air-volume air handlers' outdoor, return, mixed and supply air temperatures, supply-air setpoint, OA damper, supply airflow, heating and cooling valves, fan status and occupancy, every 15 minutes for three weeks of late spring on a fixed 55 F supply setpoint, as two units: one whose supply-air sensor reads the air and one whose sensor reads 3 F high, plus a calibrated duct logger's reading in each unit for four days.
teaches: how a sensor reading a few degrees off makes rules fire on a false reading, and why the control loop it drives looks perfect
why no check of a single trend can see a smooth, plausible offset, and what an independent reference shows
how a distrusted sensor makes every finding that reads it conditional, and the RCx report's at-risk total
publisher: CAMBER (generated locally by the user's copy)
citation: CAMBER synthetic dataset synthetic-ahu-sensor-bias, generator ahu_sensor_bias (camber.datasets._synthetic_ahu_sensor_bias), seed 108. Generated data, not measurements from any building.
timezone: naive generated clock (no DST); 15-minute samples from 2025-05-12 (a Monday) for 21 days

fault_types.sat_sensor_bias: the supply-air temperature sensor reads 3 F high; the loop holds the false reading at setpoint, so the air leaves 3 F colder. No rule's verdict is the target: the sensor comparison against the duct logger finds it

known_issues: Synthetic: generated by CAMBER's own model of two air handlers, not measured. It shows what the rules and the sensor checks see, not how a real unit behaves; never cite it as evidence about real buildings.
The LOGGER equipment holds only the duct logger's reading (four weekdays of the second week, empty otherwise); the run templates discover AHU equipment only, so no rule runs on it.
Both units hold a fixed 55 F supply setpoint where the site's design sequence resets it: a shared sequence finding, firm on the healthy unit.
